qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture two. Why evolutionary algorithms. This is about optimisation, and problems too hard to solve exactly.
Take three items. We want their weights to add up to one hundred kilograms.
Three items. Aim for 100 kg in total.
A solution is a string of bits. A one takes the item, and a zero leaves it.
Bits: 1 takes an item, 0 leaves it.
The fitness, f of s, is how far the total is from one hundred. Smaller is better.
Fitness f(s): how far from 100 kg. Smaller is better.
The simplest method is exhaustive search. It tries every possible subset.
Exhaustive search: try every subset.
With three items there are eight subsets. The best is one one zero, with f equal to five.
Try all 8: 110 is the best, with f = 5.
With three items, there are eight possible solutions.
3 items make 8 possible solutions.
Every extra item doubles that number.
Each extra item doubles the count.
A real water network has twenty-one pipes, and each pipe comes in sixteen sizes.
A real water network: 21 pipes, 16 sizes each.
Even at a billion designs a second, trying every design would take about six hundred million years.
Trying every design takes 600 million years.
A small exponential, in red, races a polynomial, in green. At first the polynomial is ahead.
A tiny exponential against a polynomial.
At n equal to forty-four, the exponential overtakes it, and it stays ahead from then on.
At n = 44 the exponential overtakes.
Now a real run, with a much bigger exponential. Sixty items, and a billion steps a second.
Now a real run, with a bigger exponential.
The polynomial, n squared, takes a few microseconds. The exponential, two to the n, takes thirty-six years.
Microseconds for a polynomial, years for an exponential.
Now a different problem. Five towns must be joined by cable, as cheaply as possible.
Connect all 5 towns as cheaply as possible.
Prim's method takes the cheapest cable that reaches a new town.
Prim: take the cheapest cable to a new town.
It keeps adding the cheapest cable, and it never makes a loop.
Keep adding the cheapest cable. No loops.
It is fast, and its answer is always the best. So this is an easy problem.
Fast and always optimal: an easy problem.
Now add a new rule. Each town may have at most two cables.
New rule: at most 2 cables per town.
But the best tree from before has three cables at town C, which is no longer allowed.
But the best tree has 3 cables at C.
So we run the same greedy method again, with the new rule.
Run the same greedy method again.
Greedy takes a cheap cable early, and that choice blocks cheaper cables later.
An early cheap choice blocks cheaper ones later.
Greedy ends at twenty, yet a tree costing nineteen exists. No fast exact method is known, so this problem is hard.
Greedy gets 20, but a tree costing 19 exists.
Nearest neighbour builds a decent tour of twenty-five cities almost instantly.
Nearest neighbour: an instant, decent tour.
The evolutionary algorithm starts from random tangles. These tours are poor.
The EA starts from random tangles.
But it keeps improving its best tour as time goes on.
It keeps improving its best tour.
Given time, it overtakes the quick method, and finds a shorter tour.
Given time, it overtakes the quick method.
This is called approximate. The answers are good, but not guaranteed to be the best.
Approximate: good answers, no guarantee.
Now the evolutionary algorithm. It starts with a population of ten solutions, each with a fitness.
A population: 10 solutions, each with a fitness.
First comes select. The fitter ones are more likely to be picked, but not only the best.
Select: fitter ones are more likely, not only the best.
Next comes vary. The children can turn out better, or worse.
Vary: children can be better or worse.
Then we must decide who stays in the population.
Next: who stays?
The first rule is to replace everyone. Now the old best can be lost.
Replace everyone: the old best can be lost.
The second rule is to merge old and new, and keep the best ten. This time the best survives.
Merge, keep the best 10: the best survives.
The third rule is to replace only the weakest. The best survives here too, and the average rises.
Replace the weakest: the best survives too.
Then the loop closes, and we go round again.
Then repeat the loop.
A fitness function gives every solution a score.
For hard problems, exact methods blow up.
So an evolutionary algorithm loops through select, vary and update, to find good answers.
